title: SLO grace and containment patterns for ML inference
author: Anika Shah
content:
Summary
=======
This document defines SLO grace, containment, and escalation patterns specific to machine-inference workloads (text generation, embeddings, and reranking). It captures pragmatic rules for when and how to allow controlled SLO degradation, how to contain tenant impact, and step-by-step actions SREs and owners must follow during high burn or capacity stress.

Scope
-----
Applies to: Redwood-hosted inference endpoints and dedicated clusters running multi-tenant inference. Not intended for private/on-prem customer-managed installs (those should follow their local contract).

Goals
-----
- Preserve availability of core inference control plane during load spikes.
- Prioritize safety: avoid noisy failures cascading to dependent systems.
- Provide clear, deterministic actions tied to measurable thresholds (SLO burn / latency / error surge).
- Optimize unit economics by favoring graceful, observable degradation patterns rather than aggressive wholesale shutdowns.

Context and motivation
----------------------
ML inference workloads have characteristics that change our SLO management compared to typical REST services: long tail latencies (esp. quantized or long-context requests), heavy token-level billing sensitivity, KV-cache volatility, and bursty traffic from generative workloads. Traditional binary circuit breakers lead to poor user experience or large financial impact. We therefore introduce graded "grace and containment" patterns that:

- apply per-tenant and per-route policies,
- progressively reduce fidelity (e.g., shorten max output tokens, fall back to smaller models, disable sampling),
- apply admission control before throttling to preserve control-plane health.

Containment pattern taxonomy
----------------------------
1) Temporal grace window
   - Short (1–5m): automatic soft-shedding that drops low-value background requests (batch embeds, async reranking).
   - Medium (5–30m): apply token caps, reduce max output length to 50% and switch to cached prefixes.
   - Extended (>30m): escalate to human review and possible tenant-level soft limit.

2) Fidelity degradation (tiered fallbacks)
   - Tier A (no degradation): p99 latency within SLO and burn rate < 2x expected.
   - Tier B (soft degrade): model variant -> smaller/quantized variant; max_tokens capped; temperature reduced for generation.
   - Tier C (hard degrade): response summarization-mode (trim long completions) or reject long-generation requests with structured error describing action.

3) Routing & capacity hedges
   - Route low-priority traffic to lower-cost preemptible pools.
   - Route high-priority traffic to reserved capacity with stricter SLO accounting.

4) Tenant impact containment
   - Fairshare throttles: ensure no single tenant exceeds N% of cluster headroom.
   - Eviction escrow: temporarily place offending tenant into a limited-rate bucket while preserving their critical control endpoints.

SLO & error-budget thresholds and automated actions
---------------------------------------------------
Table: thresholds and automatic responses. Use these as default; product teams may override for specific routes with written owner approval.

| Trigger condition | Time window | Immediate automated action | Escalation point |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| Error budget burn rate >= 3x | 5m | Soft-shed background embedding jobs; cap max_tokens=256 on chat/generation | Pager if persists 15m |
| p99 latency > target + 200ms | 5m | Switch to smaller model variant for matching route; enable cached prefix logic | SI if persists 20m |
| Token consumption surge (+200% baseline) | 10m | Reinstate token-priority admission; shift low-priority tenants to preemptible pool | OOB review if persists 30m |
| SLO violation (daily) > 0.5% | 1h | Open incident in status board + retention telemetry snapshot | Postmortem required if >1% daily |
Runbook: Containment play (operational checklist)
-------------------------------------------------
1) Verify alert and scope
   - Confirm alert via APM and the inference telemetry dashboard (latency, qps, token burn by tenant).
   - Identify impacted clusters, models, and the top-5 tenants by token burn.
2) Activate grace windows
   - Apply short grace actions automatically (token cap, model fallback). CLI example:

   rci cluster apply-policy --cluster cluster-eu-01 --policy "grace-short" --routes "chat*,embeds*"

3) Contain tenant(s)
   - Move low-priority tenants to the preemptible pool:

   rci tenant migrate --tenant-id T-1234 --pool preemptible-embeds --rate-limit 50r/s

4) Observe for 10–15 minutes. If metrics improve, maintain actions and prepare rollback plan.

5) If not improved, escalate to human oncall and consider invoking admission-control:

   rci admission enable --cluster cluster-eu-01 --policy "token-priority" --threshold 80th-percentile=150ms

6) Post-incident: collect artifacts (trace logs, sample requests, model hot-cache hit rates) and attach to incident.

Telemetry, alerts, and example queries
------------------------------------
Primary signals to instrument (per-cluster + per-model + per-tenant):
- p50/p95/p99 latency (generation token latency + first-byte)
- token_rate (tokens/s), token_burn_per_tenant (tokens/min)
- model_cache_hit_ratio (KV prefix hits)
- qps per route, dropped_requests per route
- error_budget_burn_rate (1h / 24h windows)

Example PromQL snippets (illustrative):
- p99 latency for model X:  histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(inference_latency_bucket{model="gpt-redwood-xl"}[5m])) by (le))
- token burn per tenant: sum(rate(tokens_consumed_total[1m])) by (tenant_id)
- rolling error budget burn: increase(slo_error_budget_spent_total[1h]) / increase(slo_error_budget_total[1h])

Alert guidance
- Pager: error_budget_burn_rate >= 3x for 15 minutes OR daily SLO > 1%
- Ops-only warning: p99 latency breach for 5 minutes or token spike > 200% for 10 minutes

Safety knobs and API responses
-----------------------------
- When we apply hard-degrades, return a structured HTTP 429 with JSON body containing: reason, expected duration, alternate route, and contact for support. This helps clients implement graceful retry/backoff.

JSON example: 
{ "error": "rate_limited", "reason": "token_priority_enforced", "retry_after_sec": 60, "suggested_model": "gpt-redwood-medium" }

Ownership and escalation model
-----------------------------
- Primary owners: SRE Inference team (ownership-prefix: eng-sre/inference).
- Escalation path: oncall -> inference lead -> platform infra pagers.
- Communication: update status page and incident channel within 10 minutes of human escalation.

Decision criteria for permanent remediation
-----------------------------------------
- Repeated daily soft-degrade events for a tenant (>3 times / week) -> require product/tenant engagement and quota adjustment.
- Persistent >2x baseline token consumption without business justification -> trigger billing review and capacity reserve reallocation.

Appendix A — Example automation policies
---------------------------------------
- grace-short: min_actions = [cap_max_tokens=512, prefer_cache=true, move_low_priority=false]
- fidelity-fallback: action_sequence = [model_swap: gpt-redwood-xl -> gpt-redwood-medium, temp_reduction: 0.7]

Appendix B — Incident evidence checklist
----------------------------------------
- Top-50 requests (anonymized) during the window
- Model KV cache hit rate time series (5m resolution)
- Token burn time series by tenant (1m resolution)
- Autoscaler events and preemptible pool migrations

Appendix C — Suggested SLA language for product teams
------------------------------------------------------
We recommend product teams expose:
- Route SLOs (p99 latency and availability) and token-pricing expectations.
- A documented fallback policy (what happens when we apply fidelity degradation).
